subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REPORTED WASTE IN CORPORATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the shocking reports on national television that Loto Canada may end up with bills of up to $37 million because of, in the words of our national television network, "a gamble that did not pay off', and in view of the fact that the minister was urged by the provinces and by members of the House of Commons as far back as early June not to proceed with this gamble, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That the minister make an immediate statement on motions setting out in complete detail the background of this fiasco, the reasons which motivated her, and a complete picture of the losses involved to the Canadian taxpayers so that members of the House of Commons can better understand the enormity of the blunder and ascertain, by questions after her statement, ways to prevent her from doing it again, assuming she remains in her portfolio until the spring.

speechtext:

That this House instruct the Minister of State (Environment) to resume federal funding of water quality research in Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST CORPORATION CEASE SELLING SUPPLIES TO FISHERMEN-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was originally set up to market fish from inland waters. Currently, the FFMC is also in the business of selling supplies such as nets, fuel, clothing, etc., at cost to fishermen from whom they purchase fish. In view of the fact that private companies are involved in selling supplies to fishermen, this action of the corporation is an intervention by the government into the private sector and is contrary to the marketing objectives of the FFMC.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway):
That the government take steps immediately to discontinue sales of supplies to freshwater fishermen.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the representations which I, and no doubt other members, have received with respect to Canadians presently in Iran, and in view of proposals which the Secretary of State for External Affairs apparently now has under consideration to assist citizens of Canada who may be in some difficulty in the tragic events now unfolding in Iran, can the Prime Minister indicate more specifically what contingency plans are being prepared to ensure the safety of Canadians caught in this conflict and, particularly, what steps their relatives and friends in Canada should take to ascertain their whereabouts and their circumstances?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: SAFETY OF CANADIANS IN IRAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he is preparing such contingency plans, but that at the time being there is no cause for alarm. The embassy is in touch with the some 1,200 Canadians who are in Iran. About one-third of them are in Tehran. The others are either on the Caspian or in the south where there is no immediate danger. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State (Environment) concerning the problem of phosphorus waste pollution in the Great Lakes and the production of excess algae and plant growth.
Last week the technical adviser for the Ontario environment ministry, Mr. William Steggles, stated, "some states and U.S. cities continue to pollute the lakes because no legislation controlling phosphorus levels has been passed, particularly two or three big, populous states-Ohio, Pennsylvania and Illinois-while apparently controls are being applied well on the Canadian side."
Will the minister take any measures to persuade our American neighbours to institute much more effective controls for this problem?

subsubtopic: POLLUTION OF GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the signing of the Great Lakes water quality agreement, 99 per cent of the population on the
December 5, 1978

Canadian side of the Great Lakes has been serviced by adequate sewage treatment facilities. On the American side of the Great Lakes, 65 per cent of the population is now serviced by adequate sewage treatment facilities, compared to 5 per cent when the agreement first began. So real strides are being made in this area.
Under the 1978 agreement, new final deadlines have been set by which industrial and municipal pollution control programs are to be completed and operating by December 31, 1982, and December 31, 1983, respectively. We expect to make great strides in all aspects of pollution control in the Great Lakes under this new agreement.

subsubtopic: NON-CANADIAN VESSELS-CANADIAN WATERS
speechtext:
With regard to non-Canadian registered vessels operating in Canadian waters north of the 60th parallel, how does the government ensure that such vessels meet safety and environmental standards?
December 5, 1978

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: NON-CANADIAN VESSELS-CANADIAN WATERS
speechtext:
Non-Canadian registered ships operating in any of the 16 shipping safety control zones into which the waters of the Canadian Arctic are divided pursuant to the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act are required to comply with the arctic shipping pollution prevention regulations and the arctic waters pollution prevention regulations made pursuant to that act. The former contains detailed provisions with respect to the construction, equipment, manning and navigation. To show compliance a steamship inspector may issue an arctic waters pollution prevention certificate; however, the certificate may be issued by an exclusive surveyor to a classification society if the ship is in non-Canadian waters before entry into the Arctic. A pollution prevention officer may board any ship to ensure compliance while it is in any zone. Ships report to the Arctic Canada traffic system (NORDREG Canada) which is based at Frobisher Bay. This system is at present voluntary but serious consideration is being given to make reporting compulsory.
The Arctic waters pollution prevention regulations stipulate the maximum liability of all ships entering the Arctic. In cases where a ship will be carrying more than 2,000 tons of oil, evidence of financial responsibility must be sent to the Department of Transport prior to the proposed voyage in Arctic waters, so that third party claims for clean-up costs or damage may be met.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order respecting an item in the supplementary estimates, in accordance with procedures that have been agreed to previously. I have given notice to the Chair as well as
(Mr. Speaker.]
to the House leader of the New Democratic Party and the government House leader.
My point of order is with respect to vote 30a in the External Affairs Department under the Canadian International Development Agency. It is a $1 item, something about which we have had a great deal of discussion in the past. My concern in regard to this $1 item is highlighted by the last phrase in that particular vote which authorizes to pay:
-amounts in the currency or unit of account indicated, notwithstanding that the total of such payments may exceed the equivalent in Canadian dollars estimated as of October, 1977,-
That amount is $667 million some. But this vote 30(a) is for $1, and one can see by that phrase this $1 vote grants authority to the government to exceed the amount appropriated by the main estimates of $667 million in the spring, and to exceed it by an unknown amount. One could surmise the intent of this $1 vote is that C1DA, probably for reasons of the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, has exceeded the amount appropriated for it in Bill C-61 this spring and requires additional funding.
We have established procedures and practices for handling a circumstance where spending authority has been exceeded.
If there had been anticipation of that, a contingency fund could have been appropriated, or alternatively, through supplementary estimates specific amounts could be appropriated to cover the fact that sometimes spending exceeds original estimates. In this case, for reasons that I am not clear, the government chose not to appropriate the extra amount that CIDA needs, but rather has taken the route of this $1 item to grant CIDA an unlimited authority to spend, subject to Treasury Board approval. Basically they are asking parliament to grant CIDA unlimited authority.
This is contrary to our procedures. The procedure for raising money for government operations utilizes the estimates where full disclosure as to the details and the amounts of government spending is supposed to be declared, followed by an appropriation act which appropriates a specific amount requested by Her Majesty to fulfil the responsibilities that she has. As Your Honour has ruled in the past, an appropriation act should not be used to accomplish, for example, some other legislative purpose. I submit that it should also not be used to grant open-ended authority to spend which, in a sense, is related to legislation.
If $1 votes can be used to grant open-ended authority to spend, we can easily extrapolate to a situation where the whole procedure becomes rather farcical. Rather than lay out in detail the specific amounts that are required, the government need only put down a $1 item and use that authority to spend whatever it wants to spend. That is certainly contrary to our practices and, I might add, contrary to the very strong opinion of the Auditor General in terms of the purposes of the estimates and the intent they are supposed to achieve.
If CIDA requires more funds, and we are not aware if it does or not, the procedure for the government to follow is to
December 5, 1978

request by way of supplementary estimates B, C, D or E, authority to appropriate additional funds to cover those. It is inappropriate, and I submit out of order, to ask parliament for authority to spend whatever it chooses. The government should not ask parliament for open-ended authority to spend for CIDA or any other department. It is on that basis I raise this point of order.
I have been unable to establish any precedents, in the sense that it has never occurred. 1 have done a fair amount of research. We have never had a situation where parliament has been asked to grant an open-ended authority to government by way of estimates and appropriations acts. It is certainly my understanding and I think that of everybody else, that an appropriation act should ask for a specific amount of money. It should not be open-ended. Vote 30a of the supplementary estimates of External Affairs asks for an open-ended authority to spend. I submit that should be ruled out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the question raised by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), 1 would like to assure him that there is no effort to seek open-ended authority, nor will the approval of this $1 item in the supplementary estimates provide any such open-ended authority. If my hon. friend will refer to the wording of supplementary estimates vote 30a, he will find it is precisely the same wording that is to be found in vote 30 in the main estimates. It is precisely the same amount of money that is provided in the main estimates.
There is a $1 item. In fact the estimate is increased from $667,049,909 to $667,049,910. The global amount is not increased. The ability of CIDA to spend a global amount is not increased. The $1 item provides within that global amount authority to make the expenditures that are listed in the explanation of requirement below vote 30a.
If the hon. member will look at the main estimates he will find there is a grant provided in the main estimates to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. This particular $1 vote will provide an increased grant to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in the amount of $750,000, but within the global amount that is contained in votes 30 and 30a.
The purpose of the $1 item is to seek the authority of parliament to make these grants to various international organizations within the global amount that is sought in the main estimates, and that is carried forward in the global amount plus $1 in the supplementary estimates.
1 do not believe that in any way the wording of the vote which the hon. member quoted leads to an open-ended authority. He dealt in particular with the phrase, and I quote:
-notwithstanding that the total of such payments may exceed the equivalent in Canadian dollars estimates as of October, 1977-
That is precisely the same authority that is in the main estimates. The authority sought in that expression is to convert into other currencies, with the fluctuations in the Canadian dollar. I believe that the spending authority globally is not
Point of Order-Mr. Andre
increased. What the $1 item does is authorize within the global amount these items that are listed. I hope it will be possible for the House to deal with these commendable items in the supplementary estimates.

Mr. Speaker, before the minister sits down I wonder if he would answer a question. Is he telling us that in no case will the amount spent under this item, including the supplementary, exceed $667,049,910?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is what I am saying.

Will the minister then explain what is meant by the phrase in either the main estimate or the supplementary estimate "notwithstanding that the total of such payments may exceed the equivalent in Canadian dollars." Does that total of such payments mean the total of all payments, which is what I thought it meant, or does it mean the total of certain payments inside the conglomeration?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It means the payments within the conglomeration. As I understand it, if we made a commitment with respect to a particular program in an underdeveloped country, we would be able to implement that commitment regardless of the change in the currency in which the commitment was made.

As Your Honour will realize, I am not arguing. I am trying to get this clear. Is it in effect the right to transfer some of the money from one item for which it was estimated to another item as long as it is inside the total figure? To put my over-all question again, how does the minister square the statement, whether in the main item or in the supplementary item, that there is to be no more spent than the total that has been indicated two or three times, with the statement "notwithstanding that the total of such payments may exceed the equivalent in Canadian dollars" by that much money?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am puzzled over the very wording that the hon. member has raised for the second time. In the very short time I have had available to study the matter, and to get information, I find that expression is merely a device that has been used in the main estimates, I understand, for a long time in order to permit the government to make arrangements in foreign currencies.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think perhaps this matter ought to stand over. The difficulty the Chair has is that, on the face of it, it would appear that no greater authority is being sought by the $1 item than was in fact contained in the main estimates, and that no new legislative authority is being sought by the $1 item. Therefore, in accordance with the precedents in which 1 have interfered with $1 items in the past, I would say I would not interfere with this one, because it is the proper use of a $1 item to signal the reallocation of funds that are already authorized under the estimates.

December 5, 1978
Parliament
Up to that point 1 would be prepared to accept it. However, I think we ought to satisfy ourselves currently on the meaning of the phrase about whether or not a payment under this particular authorization, either in the main estimate or the supplementary estimate, can in fact exceed the amount. That is the language which seems to trouble everybody at this point. Perhaps we might set this over until tomorrow for further clarification.
The complaint of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) is that the item contains an open-ended power. If the meaning of the words in the item is not to confer an open-ended power, there is evidently no problem. The minister has said that is not the intention. speechtext:
That this House lacks confidence in a government which for more than 15 years has deliberately and steadily undermined the fundamental function of the House of Commons and its standing committees by imposing rules and procedures of this House and its standing committees calculated and designed to stifle or eliminate parliamentary examination and control of public expenditures resulting in the steady destruction of the parliamentary process, and which has refused to undertake a serious review of House procedures or consider the numerous worth-while proposals for reform.
He said: Mr. Speaker, while you were reading the motion the parliamentary secretary interrupted and suggested you dispense with it. 1 am sure they would like to dispense totally with the opposition. It would save them a lot of trouble. We are a nuisance over on this side. They have done that in Ghana. The government there decided that the opposition was a little too vigorous, too assertive, too inquiring, so they abolished the opposition. I am sure that would be a delightful solution to all the government's critics.
This subject matter deals with the complete runaway of expenditures and the complete lack of control parliament has over those expenditures. If the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) would speak up, I will gladly entertain his questions as I go along.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I will stay, though I doubt very much if I will learn much.
The Auditor General's Report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1976, has this to say, at page 9, paragraph 2.1.
I am deeply concerned that parliament and indeed the government has lost or is close to losing effective control of the public purse. I expressed that concern a year ago in my annual report.
At page 111, paragraph 2.8, he says:
Control over public funds would appear to have been deteriorating for at least the last 15 years.
Whatever else the Auditor General has to say in his various reports over the years, the ultimate responsibility for the gross negligence and mismanagement of this country's financial affairs must lie with the ministers on the treasury benches, one of whom we are fortunate to have with us today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Two!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
They, and only they, are responsible, and they are to blame for embarking on a deliberate course of action which has resulted in so weakening the effectiveness of the parliamentary process as to render this place useless. I see another minister down the way. I am sorry I overlooked him, but the rate of change in the last ten years has been one and a half new ministers a month.
The same thing that has happened with respect to the effectiveness of this chamber has happened in the committees. I have been saying this, now, for some years. These changes have not happened overnight. They began with the Liberal government of the late Lester Pearson. A special committee was set up in March of 1964. It presented some 20 reports, the procedural aspects of which resulted in new provisional standing orders in 1965. One of the most important of these was that for the first time a limitation was placed on the proceedings dealing with financial resolutions. They were restricted to debate for one sitting day only and speeches were limited to 20 minutes, a far cry from the days when the opposition, then led by the late Mr. Pearson, held up estimates in the committee of the whole for 49 days.
Rule changes now began to appear which severely limited time for the discussion of supply. These were all provisional orders to be enforced to the end of the following session. At the time, of course, it was a minority government situation-there was no way those provisional orders would have been adopted had the government tried to force them.
Just before the election of 1968, which for the first time in a number of years returned a majority government, the one we are stuck with now, another series of reports was presented by the committee containing recommendations for changes in the rules which, for the most part, were imposed upon the House by this government with its comfortable majority. Procedure on supply was drastically changed. The year was now divided into three parts and the opposition was confined to a limited number of so-called allotted, or supply days, in each part. At the end of each of these three parts of the year, any supply business before the House must be voted upon-the guillotine.
December 5, 1978

Thus the standing committees which, by the change in the rules, now have all the estimates sent directly to them, are operating with a gun to their heads.
One of the more interesting provisions in these changes was that the operation of the standing committees, particularly in so far as the new procedures for examining estimates was concerned, was to be reviewed after they had dealt with the estimates for a time. That review has never taken place and under this government it is not likely to take place because it is far too inconvenient for the government in that it suffers no embarrassment simply because the opposition members on the committees examining the estimates are muzzled in their efforts to conduct a meaningful inquiry. 1 will come back to this in a moment.
We have, then, in this historical development, a situation where the new Liberal majority, by design, completely abolished the committee of supply. Along with that they abolished the right of the opposition to debate motions "that the Speaker leave the chair for consideration of supply." With their majority, they regiment the opposition to a restricted procedure of allotted or supply days. We must give notice of those motions, and only some of them may have a non-confidence motion attached to them.
I might digress here for a moment. They further weakened Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition by giving the right to other political parties to move motions of non-confidence, which is not in the parliamentary tradition. And, over all, there was the application of rigid time limits on debate. These developments, coupled with the abolition of appeals from Speakers' rulings, set the stage for the gradual but inevitable deterioration of the parliamentary process in controlling the public purse. The opposition is now in a straitjacket where its effectiveness in examining supply is simply non-existent.
That is what the Auditor General means when he says he is deeply concerned that parliament has lost, or is close to losing, effective control of the public purse. That is what he means when he says that control over public funds has been deteriorating for 15 years. These changes to our rules and procedures have, for all practical purposes, robbed us of the ability, procedurally, to reduce estimates. No wonder the Auditor General is deeply concerned. The control of the executive is now absolute. But then the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has always thought parliament to be a nuisance and that, when they leave the Hill, its members to be nobodies. The government has absolute control over time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Tut, tut, tut!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) says "tut, tut, tut," but I am sure he does not doubt the accuracy of these quotations. 1 just happen to have one with me here. I will just refresh his memory.
On July 25, 1969, the Prime Minister said:
1 think we should encourage members of the opposition to leave. Every time they do, the IQ of this House rises considerably.
Parliament
That is the general attitude opposite. "Get rid of the opposition. We do not need it. It is just a nuisance." The government wants to have full control so that it can travel along untrammelled in the expenditure of taxpayers' dollars.
The Prime Minister said:
-they are no longer honourable members-they are just nobodies, Mr. Speaker.
The government decides when we in the opposition will be permitted allotted days. The government really has been magnanimous in allowing six non-confidence motions in a year. In my view, the very life of this institution is threatened by that kind of attitude.
I said I would get back to the committees. What a farce they are in examining estimates! Any time the government members wish to do so-which is most of the time-they can stonewall in the committees. They are complete masters on those committees because of the government's majority.
The practice in standing committees has developed to the point where ministers-and, I am sorry to say, in many cases their officials-deliberately frame lengthy answers to questions put to them. This tactic, of course, consumes the time allotted to a member in a committee.
A question may take ten or 20 seconds to ask, and the answer of the minister takes the remainder of the five minutes allotted to a member. The chairman informs that member that his time has expired because the minister or his official has consumed the member's time in answering questions. The result is that we are stonewalled. No real examination of estimates is possible. No real explanations for expenditures are given. This single tactic of the government has done more to destroy any hope of success of standing committees in the examination of estimates than any other single factor. I am strongly suspicious that the chairmen of these committees actually go to clinics or meetings at which they are all instructed on how to handle themselves and us in the opposition in the conduct of committee affairs.
There are other factors which have contributed to the destruction of the committee system, which I say is now a farce. All committees are simply places where members can be kept occupied. Government members can be kept busy and out of the hair of ministers. With one or two exceptions, most government members do not even realize what has been done in this process of destruction. They are not able to compare the system with the system as it operated prior to 1963 or 1965 because they were not here then. They have nothing with which to compare the present system.
Prior to the changes, members were not cut off by committee chairmen-who are backed up by the government majority, which is the situation in all standing committees-because their five minutes had expired. A questioner was allowed to continue his or her line of questioning and thus was able to extract the necessary answers to his questions on the estimates. Now, as soon as government members sense that a line of questioning is getting close to embarrassing the government, the stonewalling begins, aided and abetted by chairmen who

Parliament
are, for the most part, highly partisan and just as eager to protect the backside of the government as any other government member.

I hasten to make it, and I recommend strongly to all committee chairmen, all of whom are government members, that they would do well to model their conduct as chairmen of committees after that of the hon. member for Windsor-Walk-erville (Mr. MacGuigan), who chairs the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I will put on the record just a few of the observations of the Auditor General. At page 12, paragraph 2.18 of his report of March 31, 1977, he said there was no visible action to date on recommendation that the form of the estimates be revamped so information they contain would be more meaningful and useful to parliament and would be the cornerstone for a fully effective government expenditure control system.
At page 105, paragraph 6.1 of his report of March 31, 1978, the Auditor General stressed the need to improve financial information parliament receives by improving quality of information in public accounts and estimates.
At page 105, paragraph 6.3 of his report of March 31, 1978, the Auditor General said that the information parliament receives on actual expenditures must be improved: public accounts mirror the estimates, providing little additional information.
At page 106, paragraph 6.9 of his report of March 31, 1978, the Auditor General said there was a need for improved accountability. The reports of the Auditor General are full of observations like these. At page 108, paragraph 6.18 of his March 31, 1978 report, the Auditor General said that the 1969 implementation of 15 standing committees created the need for significantly better information, which was not recognized.
With respect to expenditures, what a sad history of broken promises and deception! The Prime Minister thinks that the opposition is a nuisance. In answering a question on May 8, 1969, as recorded in Hansard at pages, 8465 and 8466, the Prime Minister said:
Apart from the continuing steps we have taken to curtail expenditure... we on this side hope that in the budgetary debate, which I take it will take place in a few weeks time,... when we announce to the country our further expenditure cuts-
Does that sound familiar? Further expenditure cuts?
-we will have the support not only of the opposition but also of the various sectors of the community. There will be a need for the government to introduce some very severe expenditure cuts which will hurt different vested interests in the country.
In the year in which the Prime Minister said that, 1969, total expenditures were $13 billion. Now total expenditures are over $52 billion. On February 18, 1970, as recorded at page 3728 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
I need not enlarge now on our determination to restrain federal expenditure, on which our intentions were put to the House when the estimates were tabled last week.
In that year, 1970, expenditures rose by another $2 billion, to $15 billion. Now', eight years later, expenditures are $52 billion.
On December 10, 1975-we are now getting more up to date-as recorded at page 9889 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
It is certain that in the meantime the government is very anxious to draw inspiration from the Auditor General's report and make sure that the government does improve the efficiency of its accounting procedures.
By the time the Prime Minister said that, expenditures had risen to $34 billion. They are now, only three years later, over $52 billion. On March 22, 1976, as recorded at page 11991 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
-the President of the Treasury Board announced two or three months ago that the federal government would seriously try to cut its expenditures, and so we have reduced the rate of growth of the Department of Public Works and of several other departments. We have also put an end to some voluntary assistance programs, like LIP.
We might add FLIP, LEAP and a few others. He continued:
We have reduced expenditures.
When he made that statement in 1976, total expenditures had risen to $41 billion, and two short years later, they are over $52 billion. It is little wonder that we and the people of Canada are rather sceptical of recently announced, so-called cuts in expenditures by the Prime Minister, and the setting up of a super ministry to co-ordinate programs of the brain children of the government which are running away with the tax dollars of Canadians.
At one time this House and its committees were a very real challenge, but no longer, not since the Liberals took office in 1963, and particularly not since the Prime Minister assumed power in 1968. At that time he immediately set about the erosion of the parliamentary process so that this place and its committees would not be a nuisance to him.

It is something which the government and opposition parties must look after, for this is not something which was imposed upon backbenchers by the government. It is something which has developed over a period of time. We should pay more attention to these things, rather than blabber on about useless motions such as the one before us today.
I am concerned about the manner in which we have proceeded with our procedural debates. The hon. member for Yukon made a totally absurd statement when he said that there has been no review of procedural changes. This is an absolute falsehood. Anybody who has been around the House of Commons for the last two and one half years and who has paid attention to what has been going on in the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, who has taken the trouble to pull out those volumes and to read them, would know what absolute bafflegab that is.
I have in my hand the proceedings of those committees. 1 had the honour to be the chairman of the subcommittee on the use of time. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was the chairman of the subcommittee on committees, and my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane), was the chairman of the subcommittee on private members' hour. We met for a period of one year. We went to England to study their system, we had hearings, and we even met when the House was not sitting, in order to consider the reports which were worked on by these bodies.
It was no surprise to me that the members in the Conservative party, members who have paid a great deal of attention to this kind of problem, such as the hon. member for Edmonton

West, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath)-none of whom are in the House at the present time-had the common sense and courtesy not to sign such a ridiculous motion.
I would like to deal with some of the charges made by the hon. member for Yukon. I am concerned about the way in which he has distorted the historical facts. I think it is clear that these reforms, when they began, did not immediately appear out of the blue. The process started with Mr. Pearson's government in 1963. It was started in 1963 because the Conservative backbenchers, under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), were totally dissatisfied with the way in which parliament was carried on and with their particular role, and so were members on this side. When the latter became the government they decided to do something about it.
A series of committees was set up and a series of experiments was carried out, culminating in the changes of 1968 to 1969. How are those changes accepted? They were accepted unanimously, without a dissenting vote, and there was not even an "on division." Those rules were not rammed down the throats of the opposition. For those members who may not wish to accept that statement at face value, I would advise them to look at the Debates and Journals of the House of Commons for December 20, 1968. They were adopted without opposition. I will not bore the House by repeating the substance of those rules, but perhaps I should remind hon. members of the result of those rules with respect to supply.
The several standing committees in the House now spend over 500 hours a year studying main and supplementary estimates, more than twice as long as was spent under the old rules in the committee of suppy on the floor of the House. That time, even though it is not spent as well as I would like to see, is surely spent far more effectively than it was on the floor of the House. If anybody doubts that, all they need do is to go back and take a look at the debates in the good old days and contrast them with even the worst committee hearings to find that there is more substance in committees today than there was in committees of the whole in the good old days.
There has been a significant improvement. It has opened up changes which allow hon. members to be more effective, and furthermore it has given them opportunities to get away from the leader syndrome which this House has always had, and has given ordinary members on both sides a greater role to play. I think we should be grateful for that.
Nobody claims that the system is perfect. Certainly I am one of those who claims that the system is in dire need of a good shakeup. As a result, after the 1974 election, the then president of the privy council and House leader, Mitchell Sharp, took on the chairmanship of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. We undertook a number of experiments, co-operatively, with members opposite, to find out how we could change the rules to make the situation more equitable and meet some of the criticisms that had been launched by members opposite. The most important of these was to permit members opposite to call for examination select-
December 5, 1978

ed items in the estimates to the committee of the whole-in other words, to go back to the good old days and to permit a vote on those items, to withdraw those items from the committee of supply and to bring them to the floor of the House of Commons and, if necessary, to have a vote.
By this experimental return to a part of the old procedures, we hoped to create a better focus on the business of supply and to give members a wider forum in which to bring forward to the House those items which they found to be wrong and about which they were concerned in the estimates.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), who did exactly that today. I think that it is an appropriate use of the standing committee and an appropriate use of the way in which the system ought to operate.
To return to the experiment, it was first tried in October, 1974, and was extended to the end of the second session of this parliament in 1976. The experiment was not continued because of the reluctance of hon. members opposite. There are still some bugs in the supply system, but to suggest that it is less effective than the old one is to ignore the facts.
I was not here at the time the hon. member for Yukon came into the House of Commons in 1957, but I have been here since 1963, and 1 am aware of how the good old days were and how the good old system operated. Having been here and having had an opportunity to absorb the old system, there was as much frustration to the other side then as there is today. I suspect that the frustration has nothing to do with what system we use to handle supply, but rather with the fact there are some members on this side of the House and some members on that side of the House, and by their performance today it is clear that the members opposite will stay opposite.

The other thing that I should point out is that a very important part of the function of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts is its ability to control its own reference at the beginning of the session. It is one of the few committees which has the staff and which is able to probe the spending of the government. It can go to work at the beginning of the session. We brought forward the Statutory Instruments Act, created the Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, and gave it authority to engage the professional staff needed to perform its important duties. This government opened those windows.
When we speak of opening windows let us speak about the greatest window opening this government has undertaken, the radio and television broadcasting of proceedings in this chamber.
For years legislative bodies toyed with the idea of broadcasting their proceedings. Most shied away from it, after considerable study. This House, at the government's request, permitted radio and television broadcasting of its proceedings on the same basis as the written Hansard. Of all possible parliamentary reforms, this certainly must be construed as the most far-reaching. It is one thing for us to meet in public and publish a printed record, but it was a different thing when we opened the House of Commons to the television cameras and to radio. Our constituents can hear us, and we know that they watch.

We dealt with the question of finding out the legislative burden that the government wanted to put through and of giving some guarantees to the government that, if we took extra time to work in our constituencies, the legislative program would be dealt with in full. There was a whole series of reforms along these lines that would have gone a long way toward achieving the point that the hon. member for Yukon was trying to make.

speechtext: The five-minute rule is not in the Standing Orders but is a rule which members imposed upon themselves.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: By a government majority.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
It is a rule imposed by members themselves at the request of members opposite. There is a great desire on the part of members on all sides of the House to see themselves as equal, and therefore they proceeded to make sure they had equal access to the floor of the committee. Hon. members have big egos, Mr. Speaker, but some members will have to decide to give way to other members of their party. It is clear that with the five-minute rule there cannot be an efficient, functioning committee. That means that backbenchers who make

December 5, 1978

up the committee system will have to make some difficult decisions. Again, it is a question of attitude.
I have been in this House almost as long as the hon. member for Yukon, Mr. Speaker, and can recall when the House of Commons used to keep more regular hours. I can also recall when parliament basically sat part-time. A session began in February, we took a break for Easter, and returned until June. If the House sat in the autumn, that was an unusual event.
In recent years we have gone to the opposite extreme. In over 13 years in the House I have seen us adjourn for the summer on the planned date only three times-in 1967, 1971, and 1978. The leader of the House held the same post on those three occasions, but I have to temper my congratulations to him. I recall that he also held that position in 1971 when the Christmas adjournment began on New Year's Eve and there was no Easter adjournment.
If parliament is to be a year-round institution, then its members will have to organize their lives in a reasonable manner. In my judgment, this means that we will have to adopt regular sitting periods that would be extended only in cases of genuine emergency.
Let us look at the implications of this. It would put the government of the day, of whatever party, in a most awkward position. The present rules would give it no guarantee that it would be able to have a decision on its legislative program. We cannot establish a system where, on the other hand, however, the government would be able to ram a huge legislative program through without parliament giving it the proper attention. That would be unwise, and I certainly would not recommend it to the House.
In the last 15 years, experience has shown that between 50 and 70 bills must be passed and are passed each year. As a veteran member, and a minister with perhaps what is a small and controllable department, I believe that proper planning and control, from cabinet level down through the public service, could easily reduce this number to 40 or 50 bills per year. I would remind the House that the government has shown some signs of improving this in the last few years.
If a legislative program of a reasonable size is to be dealt with in a limited period of time, then planning is obviously required on both sides of the House. After all, we are all human, and if we do not have incentives to make us plan, then obviously we will not do it.
I should like to propose some things that we might consider. First of all, the rules regarding management of the time of the House should require the government to produce the great bulk of its legislative program early in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. This would enable the opposition to evaluate the bills and establish its position. This, it seems to me, would be a considerable reform. I am not talking about a list of bills-I mean the actual legislation as drafted.
Parliament
Second, representatives of all parties should be able to discuss the amount of time needed for measures and agree on packaging groups of bills, or batching, if you will. We could put them into categories, for instance, major, minor, controversial, and dull, for consideration within set period of time at specified stages.
Third, some device for the government to proceed unilaterally in cases where agreement is impossible must be retained. However, my judgment, and the recommendation made by our committee on the use of time, was to head toward the British system of giving the Speaker greater authority in accepting or rejecting unilateral time limitation proposals. I am prepared to admit that we may have to seek another way because of the nature of this particular House.
Finally, I would not apply the packaging proposals to the third reading stage of major bills. It seems to me that in cases of great controversy, at the final stage the government should be willing, ready and able to take its responsibilities fully and openly. Old-fashioned closure would be the only medicine in these cases, and the government would have to take that decision along with the kudos and the problems that that brings.
The motion before us today is really an admission of failure on the part of the hon. member for Yukon who had not done his homework, had not read his debates, had not read his committee reports, and had not participated in the committee reports. The opposition is saying, through the hon. member for Yukon, that we cannot do our job, that it is the system that is to blame. Quite frankly, if I had been a minister of longer standing than I am now, I think the government could say that too from time to time. I am prepared to say that the truth lies somewhere in between. It is neither black nor white; it is probably gray. After 13 years of being enmeshed in the committee system as it has developed, I am not prepared to say it is perfect. As one of the participants in the design of some of these aspects of it, I find there is a great deal that ought to be changed, but a lot of that could be changed by the members themselves if they wish to change.
However, what I do insist upon is that we deal with the question of attitude of hon. members. There is no shortage of good ideas for reform in this place, but what there is, Mr. Speaker, is a shortage of determination on the other side to grasp the opportunities that are available to them.

Eiaving said a nice word or two to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, I should like to correct one impression that he gave when he talked about the package of rules that was adopted in 1968 and 1969. He went on at great length and used his finest oratory to stress the point that the package that was passed in December, 1968, was passed without a dissenting vote. May I remind him, sir, that there was a lot in that package that was very objectionable and very offensive. It was because the government withdrew portions of what had been put before the House in 1968 that the House accepted the rest of it without a dissenting vote. But one has to look at the package as a whole.
The portion that was withdrawn in December, 1968, came back in June of 1969, I believe, in the form of rules 75A, 75B and 75C, and one of those summers that my friend did not like staying here was that summer of 1969 when that remaining part of the 1968 package was debated and put through under closure. So I say to my hon. friend, do not give us the impression that the package offered in 1968 was that happily received. Part, as I say, had to be put under the closure rule which the Tories brought in back in 1913. One of the troubles around this place is that too often the Liberals take their cue from the Tories, and that was one of the times when they used that old Tory closure rule.
Having said that about the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations, may I say a word about the motion and the speech made on it by the mover. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES

I can also say that I do not agree with all of the things which the hon. member for Yukon has said in his speech. I want to say, and perhaps I shall come to this in a little more detail

in a moment or two, that I think it is a better place today than it was in the so-called good old days.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: My two friends who have spoken ahead of me have vied with each other as to which one of them was in a position to talk about the good old days. But they are only talking of 13, 15 or 20 years of being around here. I first visited this place as a teen-age student, 54 years ago and first came here as a member 36 years ago.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I bow to you, sir.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
So I do know a bit about the good old days. Mind you, I am going to divide what I have to say about the good old days into two parts. I am going to assert that things are better now than they were then, but there is one respect in which they were better many years ago. Perhaps I might indicate some of the things I think have made this place a better institution than it used to be.
My friend from Yukon told the hon. member across the way that he did not remember the days before the microphones hung from the ceiling. He said in those days there was more freedom of debate. Well, I can go back to the days when there were no microphones at all in this place.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: There were no lights.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Those are the good old days 1 want to go back to.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
You had to be
heard by the sound of your own voice. Many members tried it once and did not try again. I notice now that if the electricity goes off this place comes to a standstill.
When I first came here, I sat in the back row. There was no electronic equipment of any kind. I had to be heard by the sound of my own voice. It was nicer for some of us. In our party we all seemed to have good voices. At least we had lots of nerve, or whatever it took, and we were all participants. However, the two old parties seemed to have 25 or 50 milquetoasts. They would make one speech in the session and find it so difficult to be heard that they gave up. That was fine for us.
We did not get caught in these quotas as to time. We were able to make all the speeches we wanted to make. But I think this is a better parliament because there is more participation. It is better not just because of television but because of the microphones that were brought in here. That innovation made more of a change in parliament than anything I have seen since I have been here, even more than television. Once the microphones were brought in, they produced an equality in terms of being heard. From that day on, the participation by all members has increased greatly. In that sense, it is a better place than it used to be.
In terms of the rules, we have made a number of changes which make this a better place. I like what we did with regard
December 5, 1978

to statements by ministers which we used to call statements on motions. That is not the correct term now. It is statements on statements.
In the old days, every time a minister made a statement there had to be an argument as to whether anybody had a right to reply and, if so, how many. There were no questions. We resolved that. We provided, by rule, that when a minister makes a statement one spokesman from each party can reply and there can be a question period. It may have reduced the number of statements that are made, but the handling of those statements is much better under the present rule than it was under the old.
The institution of "the late show" was beneficial to the operation of this place. Under the old system, members got put down when their questions were out of order. They had to wait for months for some grievance spot to raise something. With the institution of "the late show," if a member is not satisfied with an answer in the question period, it is possible to get on one of nine spots during the week after ten o'clock. I have noticed in changes in the rules that have been made since "the late show" was introduced that it has not been abolished. I think the Chair likes it as well. Mr. Speaker knows that if he puts a member down, that member has a right to get on "the late show".
We have improved our handling of legislation by the method of sending bills, with the exception of tax bills, to a standing committee, then establishing as we did the report stage. Back in the so-called good old days, all bills were dealt with here in committee of the whole. On occasion we would send a bill to a committee. If we did that, when it came back to committee of the whole, we went over it again. Usually members on the standing committee learned something about the bill while it was in progress. When it came back to committee of the whole, they could talk longer than if it had not been to the standing committee. I can give you chapter and verse. It happened quite often.
We now send bills to a standing committee, but we have the report stage here. At the report stage we do not have every clause called as we did in the old committee of the whole set-up. Instead members have to put down their amendments to specific clauses in the bill. In other words, the rights of hon. members who are not on the standing committee are reserved. They can deal with the parts of the bill they are concerned with here on the floor of the House.
In many of these respects, this place has improved. The introduction of television and radio broadcasting of the proceedings of this House is good. We get a lot of complaints. One of the biggest complaints last year was that people did not like the desk thumping. The Tories have tried to correct that by applauding, using their hands. We will have to wait a while to see what the Gallup poll says as to which people like, thumping desks or clapping hands.
The odd thing is that even though people criticize parliament from what they see over television, they seem to want more of it. The broadcasting people tell us there is more and more demand for the question period and other parts of this
Parliament
show to appear over television. I am told it even upstages some of the soap operas during the day. That did not happen in the good old days. I think this is good.
I could go on. I welcome the points that the hon. member across the way made about the opportunities of the facilities that are made available to members to do their job. When I came here, we were given a railway pass which we could use as often as we wanted. We still get it. We got our berth and meals, our expenses for making trips home by train. How often? Twice a year. Now we get 52 air trips a year. Don't tell me about the good old days.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: They were the good old days.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
In one sense they were. We were not expected to be travelling all over the country all the time.
The free printing, the free telephone, constituency offices, and all the other things that members have had provided to them in order to do their job are a hundredfold better than they were in the so-called good old days.
I must not spend all my time in this way. As I say, in most instances, it is a better parliament now than it was 36 years ago. I look forward to its being a still better parliament in 36 years from now for any of us who may still be here. There is one respect, and I come to this because it is at the heart of this motion, in which I think we did do a better job, not in what my two predecessors referred to as the olden days, but in the olden days to me, back in the forties and fifties. That is with regard to estimates.
Those were the days when all estimates were dealt with in committee of supply. There were no time limits. We used to have long debates, even to get the Speaker out of the chair to get into committee of supply. Those were grievance occasions. However, every estimate had to be dealt with in committee of supply.
Some members who go back a few years may recall an interim period when we dealt with estimates here. However, there was a time limit. The result was a minister stood or sat over there and heard his estimates discussed. He did not worry about them. He knew they went to the bottom of the list and, when the last day came, they were called without further discussion.
Back in the old days when the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) sat in the gallery and watched the show, young boy that he was in those days, there was no time limit. Members could deal with estimates as they wanted. Sometimes when you got to a time when it looked as though they were going to go through and you started to slide down the estimates, and calling them one by one and passing them, all of a sudden John Blackmore would get up and we would spend a couple more hours on them. Maybe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would do the same. The result was we could hold ministers at bay, saying they could not get their estimates until they gave us some satisfaction on some point. I think it was better.

December 5, 1978
Parliament
Some members may ask why we changed it. We changed it because we had to do so. The amount of money that parliament had to deal with had multiplied manyfold. The amount of things in which parliament got involved was extended considerably, everything in the social security field, the science field, and international affairs.
There are all kinds of things that parliament is in today that we did not have in the old days. If I may speak from my own experience as one interested in a field all members know about, there was no Department of National Health and Welfare. Before the days of my good friend across the way, and thank God we have it and have her-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
That was just to embarrass her. In those days, old age pensions were an item in the estimates of the Minister of Finance. When did we get to that item? Usually in the last two or three days of the session.
There were no family allowances. Earlier than that, there was no unemployment insurance, no guaranteed supplement, no Canada Pension Plan, and no health estimates of any kind. The point I am making is that things which are now the responsibility of a very large department, the Department of National Health and Welfare, just weren't there.
Because the number of things we were involved in became so extensive, we reached the point at which we realized we could not go on giving unlimited time to every item in the book. So parliament experimented. For a while we experimented with the idea of a certain number of days, something in the order of 30 or 35 days. Well, that seemed sensible. It was not many fewer days than we had been taking previously. But once we had started it we found it didn't work because the minister would sit there and let his estimates be discussed for a day or two days at the most, and that would be all. He didn't have to satisfy anybody. He knew that on the thirty-fifth day or whenever it was, his estimates would be called and would be passed. So that did not suit.
There was also a period when we had a committee on estimates. We tried that for two or three sessions. It didn't work very well either. In 1968 we came up with this idea of sending the estimates each to an appropriate committee and getting them off the floor of the House altogether. 1 do not think it is working. My friend across the way doesn't defend it either. We just haven't found a solution to the problem of parliamentary control over the spending of moneys in this place. I think we have to stay with it until we do, and I think it is perfectly proper that the House should vote non-confidence in the government for not having come up with a solution to this problem. Don't tell me it was in the package that was produced a year or so ago, because it wasn't.
I do not presume, after all this, to say I have the answer, but I know there are some things that should happen. The estimates should be given to us in much greater detail. The block global figures we get do not mean a thing to us. In those good

old days there was more detail. You could find the matter you wanted to talk about by going through the book. The book was a lot thinner then than it is now, but there was a lot more in it.
The other thing we should try, bearing in mind that even in this modern age there are still only 12 months in a year and that there is not time to deal with everything in detail, is a selective arrangement whereby in each year during which parliament sits we could deal with four or five departments only. The government should not know in advance what those departments are; it should be the right of the opposition each year to say which departments will be called. And if we had to reduce the number from five to four, to three or what have you, so that we can deal with those departments on the floor of the House, without time limit, I would say we should make that decision. The part of the old system which did work was that the House could hold the minister at bay until he either corrected an estimate, dropped it, or gave a satisfactory answer.
I think the reason the Auditor General is in a position to say the kind of things he said in his recent report is because the way we handle our estimates today is really a farce. I have said this in the context of having been frank enough to say that I think many of our rules have been improved. But on this score we are so far from reality that we might almost as well drop the consideration of estimates altogether.
It is on that basis my colleagues and I are prepared to vote for this motion, as an expression of non-confidence in the government for not having found a way to cope with the estimates. I do not want to be viewed as one who is criticizing what has been done without having an alternative to offer. 1 would be happy to listen to other suggestions, but most of those who have thought about this subject think more or less along this line-I believe the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations does. As a matter of fact, he may have been cribbing a bit from some of my ideas when he proposed the same general approach to legislation.
I have suggested many times that the government should be required at the start of a session to list all the bills it proposes to bring in, that there should be a conference among the representatives of the parties, that the bills should be categorized as important, semi-important, unimportant or unnecessary, or dull, as the minister called them. Then we should reach agreement as to time limit on the bills that are unimportant and so on.
I see that you are looking at me, Mr. Speaker. Would you pardon me for a moment. I had forgotten we were limited to 20 minutes; I was thinking of 30. I shall wind up right away.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: It is strange around here, the things to which you can get agreement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Turn off the lights and mikes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTIONPARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
If the mikes are turned off, Mr. Speaker, I still know how to speak up. I think
December 5, 1978

things that are important and serious should be debated without time limit, but the unimportant should be got through, and in the same vein I come back to estimates and say we should find a means whereby we deal each year with three or four or five departments picked by the opposition, and give them the works.
I must sit down, Mr. Speaker. I should just like to say that, important as I believe procedure to be, it is not the whole problem around here. A large part of the problem has to do with attitudes, with confrontation; another problem is lack of substance in the legislation the government brings forward. We could have the best rules in the world, but with a government which will not cope with unemployment or inflation, well, where are you? Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me this extra minute or two.
